To verify that $f(x,y)$ is a valid joint probability density function, we must check the following conditions:

- $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}$

- ${∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y=1$

First, let's sketch the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x<2y\le 2}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069972/assets/60acb4126a456e51e00db8bbeb2f8dbc6a773a4792dda7838d2aa6a3553fa739.png)

Now, let's check our conditions:

- Since $c>0,$ we clearly have $f(x,y)\ge 0$ for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2}.$ So the first condition is satisfied.

- For the second condition to be satisfied, we must have 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2y}c{e}^{x-y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=1.
$$

$$
{∬}_{{R}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2y}c{e}^{x-y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=1.
$$

We evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating  $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2y}c{e}^{x-y}\,dx\,dy & =c{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-y}[{\int }_{0}^{2y}{e}^{x}\,dx]dy \\  & =c{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-y}[{e}^{x}]_{x=0}^{x=2y}\,dy \\  & =c{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-y}({e}^{2y}-{e}^{0})dy \\  & =c{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{y}-{e}^{-y})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}c{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{y}-{e}^{-y})\,dy & =c[{e}^{y}+{e}^{-y}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =c({e}^{1}+{e}^{-1})-({e}^{0}+{e}^{0}) \\  & =c(e+{e}^{-1}-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
c(e+{e}^{-1}-2)=1\,⇒\,c=\frac{1}{e+{e}^{-1}-2}.
$$
